To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the surface stress effects can have a significant impact on both the critical epitaxial thickness and the partitioning of misfit strain between volume elastic strain and the interfacial dislocations.

the surface stress of the free surface of an epitaxial film is the dominant driving force for dislocation nucleation in thin films, and that the interface dislocation density is determined by the balance of the surface stress of both the free surface and interface.

the critical thickness for the onset of misfit dislocations in thin films is determined by the competition of the surface stress and the elastic strain energy in the film, and that the surface stresses of free surface and the interface can be used as a tool to control the critical thickness of thin films.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new class of thin-film materials with novel electronic, magnetic, optical, and mechanical properties, and with the elucidation of the fundamental physics of the growth of these materials.
the thermodynamics of thin films, with emphasis on surface and interface stresses.
the study of the fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic processes that govern the growth and properties of thin films.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the thermodynamic theory of epitaxy in a thin epitaxial film on a substrate is not well developed and that further work is required to clarify the role of the surface stresses in the thermodynamics of thin films.
the surface stress effects on the epitaxial growth of thin films are important and must be included in the thermodynamics of the epitaxy.
the thermodynamics of the epitaxial system is a function of both the volume elastic strain energy of the film and the interface energy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of surface stress are to lower the critical thickness for the onset of misfit dislocations and to increase the number of misfit dislocation segments per unit length of interface.
the effects of surface stresses are important and must be included in any quantitative theory of epitaxy.
, in addition to the surface stress effects, the thermodynamics of the epitaxial system must also be described by a free energy function which depends on the film thickness and the misfit strain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of a free surface or an interface, the critical thickness for coherent epitaxy would be much larger than it is.
the surface stresses of both the free surface and film-substrate interface can have an important effect on epitaxy, and should not be ignored.

the surface stress effects on the critical thickness are significant for a large class of systems, while the effects on the partitioning are important only in the limit where the misfit strain is small.
